title: Ivana Trump Physical and Sexual Abuse During Marriage
description_short: Ivana Trump Physical and Sexual Abuse During Marriage
description_medium: Ivana Trump’s 1990 divorce deposition described an encounter with Donald Trump as rape; he denied the allegation. In a 1993 clarification, she said she had used “rape” to describe feeling violated, not to make a literal or criminal accusation. In 2015, she called the story “without merit.” The available accounts differ, and no adjudicated finding is cited.
description_long: During her 1990 divorce proceedings, Ivana Trump described an encounter with Donald Trump after scalp surgery and used the word “rape,” according to reporting by The New Yorker and ABC News. Donald Trump denied the allegation. Ivana later clarified in a 1993 statement that she had not meant “rape” in a literal or criminal sense, but to describe feeling violated. In 2015, she called the story “without merit.” These accounts record a serious allegation, a denial and later statements that qualify how Ivana described the encounter; they do not establish a court finding that an assault occurred. The supplied sources also do not support the preserved draft’s claims that she recanted under pressure, was silenced by a confidentiality agreement or experienced a documented pattern of physical abuse. The entry should distinguish the original deposition from Ivana’s later clarifications rather than state the allegation as an established finding. A fuller account of the deposition and the agreement governing public statements would be needed before describing the legal or personal circumstances around her later comments.

preserved_fields.title: Ivana Trump Physical and Sexual Abuse During Marriage
preserved_fields.description_short: Ivana Trump Physical and Sexual Abuse During Marriage

notes: Missing context: full deposition and any agreement or records governing Ivana Trump’s later public statements. The linked accounts document an allegation, Trump’s denial, Ivana’s 1993 clarification and her 2015 statement; they do not establish an adjudicated finding or the preserved draft’s coercion and silencing claims. Proposed correction: frame the entry as an allegation and identify the later clarifications.

title: Trump: Chad Wolf warns that Russia (and only Russia) is interfering in the election
description_short: Trump: Chad Wolf warns that Russia (and only Russia) is interfering in the election
description_medium: At a September 2020 Senate hearing, Acting Homeland Security Secretary Chad Wolf said Russia was actively interfering in the U.S. election. He distinguished that activity from threats posed by China and Iran, saying intelligence did not then show they had carried out attacks. Wolf also said Russia sought to denigrate Joe Biden. His statement addressed activity at that time, not the absence of other foreign threats.
description_long: Acting Homeland Security Secretary Chad Wolf told senators in September 2020 that Russia was actively engaged in election interference and sought to denigrate then-candidate Joe Biden. He also said the United States faced election-related threats from China and Iran, while stating that intelligence did not show those countries had yet carried out attacks. The distinction was between an identified active operation attributed to Russia and threats or motives involving other governments. The linked Trump File account also noted earlier public claims about China and Iran, but those claims referred to a National Counterintelligence and Security Center assessment that the countries had reasons to prefer Biden, not that they were already trying to change the election result. Wolf’s testimony therefore did not mean Russia was the only country posing a threat. The source links his remarks to earlier disputes over DHS handling of Russian interference warnings, but the hearing statement itself documents what he told Congress. It does not establish why his characterization differed from the broader threat assessment or prove that political pressure caused a change in his public position.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: Chad Wolf warns that Russia (and only Russia) is interfering in the election
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: Chad Wolf warns that Russia (and only Russia) is interfering in the election

title: Trump: Russia stands by Trump contesting the U.S. election
description_short: Trump: Russia stands by Trump contesting the U.S. election
description_medium: After Joe Biden was projected to win the 2020 election, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russia would wait for an official result before recognizing a winner or congratulating him. Peskov cited Donald Trump’s announced legal challenges and contrasted the situation with Russia’s quick congratulations to Trump in 2016. The statement documented Moscow’s position at that moment, not endorsement of every Trump lawsuit.
description_long: On November 9, 2020, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russia would wait for an official U.S. election announcement before recognizing a winner or congratulating Joe Biden. Asked why Vladimir Putin had congratulated Donald Trump soon after the 2016 election, Peskov said the situations differed because Trump had announced legal procedures challenging the 2020 result. The statement came after major U.S. news organizations projected Biden as the winner and while Trump’s campaign pursued court challenges. Russia was among the major countries that had not yet congratulated Biden. Peskov’s comments explained the Kremlin’s stated reason for waiting; they did not show that Russia endorsed the merits of each lawsuit or that the legal challenges would change the result. The supplied account does not describe a later recognition announcement or establish whether Russia’s delay affected U.S. proceedings. The documented event is a public diplomatic statement about recognition and congratulations during the interval between projection and formal certification, rather than evidence of Russian participation in Trump’s legal effort.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: Russia stands by Trump contesting the U.S. election
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: Russia stands by Trump contesting the U.S. election

notes: Peskov said Russia would wait for an official announcement and pointed to Trump’s legal challenges. The statement does not establish Kremlin endorsement of every challenge.

title: Trump: Texas asks Supreme Court to overturn the election results in four states, White House involved
description_short: Trump: Texas asks Supreme Court to overturn the election results in four states, White House involved
description_medium: Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton asked the Supreme Court to invalidate election results in Georgia, Michigan, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin, arguing that their voting procedures were unconstitutional. More than 100 House Republicans and 17 state attorneys general later supported the suit. The Court rejected it, finding Texas had not shown a legally cognizable interest in how other states ran their elections. The linked account says lawyers close to the White House helped draft the filing.
description_long: On December 8, 2020, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton filed a lawsuit asking the Supreme Court to block the certification of presidential election results in Georgia, Michigan, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. Texas argued that changes to voting procedures in those states were unconstitutional and sought to prevent their electoral votes from being counted. More than 100 House Republicans and 17 other state attorneys general later supported the effort. The Supreme Court rejected the case, stating that Texas had not demonstrated a judicially cognizable interest in how another state conducted its elections. The linked account says lawyers close to the White House helped draft the filing, but the materials do not identify those lawyers or show that Trump personally directed the lawsuit. The case sought a remedy affecting votes in four states after they had reported their results; it did not succeed in court. The event is significant as an attempt by one state to challenge other states’ election administration, followed by the Court’s rejection on standing grounds. The result left the states’ certified outcomes in place.

title: Trump tweets from official POTUS account to attack Twitter & Section 230
description_short: Trump tweets from official POTUS account to attack Twitter & Section 230
description_medium: After Twitter permanently suspended his personal account on January 8, 2021, Donald Trump posted from the official @POTUS account to criticize Twitter, call for repeal of Section 230 and discuss building another platform. Twitter removed the posts almost immediately. CNBC reported that the company’s reason for removing the @POTUS posts was unclear.
description_long: On January 8, 2021, Twitter permanently suspended Donald Trump’s personal account, citing the risk of further incitement of violence. Later that day, Trump used the government-owned @POTUS account to criticize Twitter, accuse its employees of coordinating with Democrats to silence him, renew his call to strip Section 230 protections from technology companies and say his team was exploring a new platform. CNBC reported that the @POTUS posts were removed almost immediately, though it was unclear what steps Twitter took in handling that account. Trump’s personal-account suspension followed his January 6 posts and the attack on the Capitol; the official-account messages did not restore his access to Twitter’s personal service. The episode involved posts made using the presidential account after the platform suspended his own account, and the posts disappeared shortly after publication. The article does not provide an archive of all messages or identify why each was removed. It documents Trump’s public objection and platform plans, not whether a separate service was ultimately created or how Section 230 policy changed.
subcategory: Use of official account after platform suspension

preserved_fields.title: Trump tweets from official POTUS account to attack Twitter & Section 230
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump tweets from official POTUS account to attack Twitter & Section 230

notes: CNBC dates the posts to January 8 and says they were removed almost immediately; the linked timeline is dated one day later. The reason for removing the @POTUS posts was unclear in CNBC’s account.

title: Trump: Pence meets with GOP House members, planning organization to defend Trump presidency
description_short: Trump: Pence meets with GOP House members, planning organization to defend Trump presidency
description_medium: Former Vice President Mike Pence met with Republican Study Committee members for two hours on February 23, 2021. He spoke positively about Donald Trump and said he planned to launch an organization to defend the Trump-Pence administration’s record. The supplied account does not name the group or document whether it was later formed, so the event is the meeting and announced plan.
description_long: On February 23, 2021, former Vice President Mike Pence met with members of the Republican Study Committee, a group of House Republicans, for about two hours in his transition office. Pence spoke positively about Donald Trump and told the members he planned to launch an organization focused on defending the Trump-Pence administration’s record. A participant said Pence discussed what he would do next and that the effort would address the administration’s record and the role House Republicans had played. The available account does not name the organization, describe its funding or structure, give a launch date or establish what activities followed. The meeting took place after the Trump administration had left office and appears in the record as part of Pence’s plans for its public defense. It documents a private discussion and an announced intention, not a completed organization or a campaign that had already begun. Without subsequent records, the plan’s scope and outcome remain unknown.

preserved_fields.title: Trump: Pence meets with GOP House members, planning organization to defend Trump presidency
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump: Pence meets with GOP House members, planning organization to defend Trump presidency

title: Trump: J.D. Vance wants to track women seeking abortions
description_short: Trump: J.D. Vance wants to track women seeking abortions
description_medium: In June 2023, Senator J.D. Vance and other lawmakers urged HHS Secretary Xavier Becerra to oppose a Biden administration HIPAA rule limiting disclosure of reproductive-health records to law enforcement. The letter argued the policy interfered with enforcement of state abortion laws. The supplied account does not quote a direct Trump statement or establish a system for tracking pregnancies.
description_long: Senator J.D. Vance and several conservative lawmakers wrote to Health and Human Services Secretary Xavier Becerra on June 16, 2023, objecting to a Biden administration rule that restricted law-enforcement access to reproductive-health records. The letter argued that the policy exceeded HHS authority and impeded enforcement of state laws governing abortion. The linked account says the rule covered records related to reproductive care such as fertility treatment, contraception and miscarriage, and restricted disclosures of that information for investigations into legally provided care. The lawmakers sought to block that privacy protection; their letter did not create a pregnancy-monitoring system. The account’s headline describes the position as wanting to track women seeking abortions, but the supplied material does not show a specific proposal for a new tracking database or its implementation. It also states that Trump supported “abortion surveillance programs” in 2024 without providing a direct quotation or identifying a policy. The 2023 letter documents Vance’s position, while Trump’s connection and the scope of the claimed surveillance proposal need direct sourcing before they can be stated as fact.
organization_tags: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services

title: Hydroxychloroquine Death Push - Deadly Drug Promotion
description_short: Hydroxychloroquine Death Push - Deadly Drug Promotion
description_medium: In March 2020, Trump publicly promoted hydroxychloroquine as a possible COVID-19 treatment, calling it a “game changer” and asking, “What do you have to lose?” The FDA later revoked emergency authorization for chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine for certain hospitalized COVID-19 patients, saying the drugs were unlikely to help and posed serious cardiac risks. The supplied evidence does not link Trump’s remarks to particular deaths or shortages.
description_long: During the early COVID-19 response in March 2020, Donald Trump promoted hydroxychloroquine as a possible treatment, calling it a “game changer” and asking what patients had to lose. The remarks encouraged public attention to a drug that had not been shown to work against COVID-19, while clinicians and researchers were still evaluating its safety and effectiveness. On June 15, the Food and Drug Administration revoked emergency authorization for chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine from the Strategic National Stockpile for certain hospitalized patients. The agency said the drugs were unlikely to be effective for those uses and that potential serious cardiac adverse events meant known and potential risks outweighed benefits. The FDA notice addresses the drugs’ authorized emergency use; it does not establish that Trump’s promotion caused specific deaths, shortages for patients with lupus or rheumatoid arthritis, or any particular treatment decision. Nor does the supplied material identify deaths caused by hydroxychloroquine during the period. The record supports describing the president’s public promotion and the later regulatory reassessment, while the title’s claim of a “death push” and the preserved draft’s causal claims require additional evidence.
subcategory: Promotion of an unproven COVID-19 treatment

preserved_fields.title: Hydroxychloroquine Death Push - Deadly Drug Promotion
preserved_fields.description_short: Hydroxychloroquine Death Push - Deadly Drug Promotion

notes: The FDA notice supports its June 15 revocation and stated efficacy/risk assessment. It does not establish that Trump’s remarks caused specific deaths, shortages or treatment outcomes; the title’s causal framing is not demonstrated by the supplied evidence.
